summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Pegasus Labs through the Console's usage analytics, per-route dashboards, and cost decomposition. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated capacity with FinOps targets; key asks: security docs, pilot runbook, and a benchmark using their route definitions.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-02-02 16:00 UTC | Duration 46m | Attendees: Alex Mercer, Priya Nair (Redwood) — James Park, Lina Morales, Omar Reyes, Sofia Chen (Pegasus Labs)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick demo focused on console usage insights and per-route cost breakdown; questions about VPC/private deployment, SSO and unit economics.

[00:00] Alex Mercer: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Alex here from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How are you all doing?
[00:10] James Park: Good, thanks. Excited to see the console — we're trying to understand where inference spend is coming from.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Great. Quick agenda — we'll start with high-level usage analytics, then drill into per-route dashboards and cost decomposition, and finish with how Optimize suggests batching/quantization changes. Feel free to jump in.
[00:33] Lina Morales: Sounds good. One note: we have two main routes, "user-facing chat" and "batch-embed", and a background reranking job. We'll want to see per-route attribution.
[00:45] Alex Mercer: Perfect, that's what we'll show. Priya, can you share the console?
[00:52] [screen share starts]
[01:03] Priya Nair: Ok I'm on the Console > Usage page. Top chart is tokens over time, then the routes table. You can see the default time window is 30 days. I'm going to filter to Pegasus Labs account and then to production namespace.
[01:20] [01:20] Priya Nair: Here are the route-level cards. Notice the chat route is 62% of tokens but only 48% of cost because it's mostly short responses; batch-embed is 30% of tokens but 40% of spend because embeddings on our larger model are more costly. There's also a small rerank route that spikes at midnight due to nightly jobs.
[01:45] Omar Reyes: Wait, embeddings more costly per token? Is that due to model choice or sequence length?
[01:51] Priya Nair: Mostly model choice — embeddings use our embedding model which runs at a higher per-request unit cost; also batch requests have less amortized KV cache benefit. In the console you can click into a route to see model, quantization, and token distribution.
[02:10] [02:10] Priya Nair: Opening the "chat" route detail. Top panel: latency percentile heatmap, below that is token distribution and cost breakdown. See this toggle for cost view: nominal cost vs normalized cost per 1k requests. You can also slice by model variant (e.g., gpt-like-open vs redwood-compact).
[02:30] James Park: How accurate are those cost numbers? We run internal chargebacks so we need predictable mapping to cloud spend.
[02:37] Alex Mercer: The Console uses Redwood's unit economics model tied to instance-hours, token throughput, and model kernel selection. We show both raw platform cost and an adjusted estimated cloud equivalent. It's not a bill, but very close. We can export the route-level CSV for your FinOps team.
[02:56] Lina Morales: Export would help. Also curious about the prefix caching note you mentioned in the email — can we see cache hit stats per route?
[03:03] Priya Nair: Yep — under the request breakdown you can toggle cache metrics. For chat, our prefix cache hit is around 18% which reduces token compute on repeat prompts. For the batch-embed route it's near 0 because each embedding input is unique.
[03:20] [03:20] Priya Nair: Now I'll jump to the "Optimize suggestions" panel. This flags routes with high per-token cost and suggests batching, lower-precision quantization, or swapping to a smaller model with a quality delta estimate based on your evalset. For example, it suggests 4-bit quant on redwood-compact for background rerank — estimated 28% cost reduction and minimal quality loss per our eval.
[03:48] Omar Reyes: That 28% is attractive. How do we verify quality before switching? We need a canary or A/B path.
[03:54] Priya Nair: Absolutely — Console supports rollout policies. You can create an A/B route split and set automatic rollback on a quality regression metric or latency SLO breach. We can instrument your eval prompt set to run during pilot.
[04:10] Sofia Chen: Security question — if we go dedicated or private, how much of this console telemetry remains in Redwood vs our VPC?
[04:18] Alex Mercer: Great Q. For Dedicated, metrics are isolated to your tenant but stored in our managed telemetry; for Private (VPC/on-prem) the control plane is customer managed and telemetry can be configured to stay in your environment and point to your KMS for encryption. We have SOC 2 and detailed audit logs — I'll send the security pack after the call.
[04:40] James Park: Is SSO supported? We use Okta and need SCIM for provisioning.
[04:46] Priya Nair: Yes, SAML SSO + SCIM and RBAC are supported. We'll include sample SSO config and minimum roles for FinOps and SRE.
[04:56] [05:00] Priya Nair: Back to route cost — here's a drill into the rerank job. You can see hourly spikes; clicking any spike shows the underlying request traces and which model variant and kernel was used. That helps root cause sudden cost jumps.
[05:20] Lina Morales: We often see a nightly surge from a scheduled ETL. Could we set an autoscaling policy or pre-warm to reduce tail latency?
[05:28] Alex Mercer: Yes, Dedicated allows reserved capacity with configurable burst and pre-warm windows. Console suggests autoscale policies and shows expected cost vs latency tradeoffs.
[05:38] Omar Reyes: Side question — we compare Redwood to managed endpoints on AWS, will the Console help us show cost delta to Bedrock or running our own endpoints?
[05:46] Priya Nair: We have a benchmark export and a cost comparison sheet — we'll run your traffic through our replay tool and produce a normalized cost comparison to Bedrock and self-hosted. Keep in mind model variants and kernel differences cause some delta.
[06:05] [06:05] Priya Nair: Now demoing the alerts: you can set budget alerts per route with thresholds on nominal spend or token rate. Also anomaly detection flags unusual per-token cost increases.
[06:22] James Park: That anomaly detector — is it customizable? We have some planned promos that spike usage legitimately.
[06:28] Priya Nair: You can set suppression windows or create expected patterns. Also define labeling so promotions map to a campaign route.
[06:36] [06:36] Alex Mercer: Quick poll — are you leaning hosted, dedicated, or private for the pilot?
[06:42] James Park: We're leaning hosted for the pilot to move fast, but dedicated if costs and isolation match our targets.
[06:49] Omar Reyes: FinOps wants target unit cost under $0.004 per 1k tokens for production — that's our rough target.
[06:59] Priya Nair: Noted. We'll include model/quantization suggestions that hit that target where possible and show tradeoffs.
[07:08] [07:08] Priya Nair: Wrapping up — I'll create a sample pilot config: route definitions, eval prompts for quality checks, and autoscale settings. We'll run a 3-day replay and share the report.
[07:20] Lina Morales: One more thing — can we map routes to our internal charge codes?
[07:25] Alex Mercer: Yes, tags and labels can be added to routes and reflected in exports for chargebacks.
[07:32] James Park: Ok, let's reconvene after you send the pilot runbook. Thanks both.
[07:36] Alex Mercer: Thanks all — we'll follow up with docs and pricing.
[07:40] [screen share ends]

Recap / commitments: Redwood to send security pack, pricing, pilot runbook, and schedule run for 2027-02-09. Action owners captured in action_items.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attribution and filler words retained; some product names transcribed differently (e.g., "redwood-compact" sometimes as "redwood compact").

End of meeting.
